## What you just did, as diagrams
:::

```{=html}
<div id="l4-explain" class="lx-xgrid">
<div class="lx-fallback">
<dl class="lx-ideas">
<dt>Day-ahead forecast</dt><dd>The operator's estimate of every hour of tomorrow's demand, used to schedule plants.</dd>
<dt>Forecast error</dt><dd>Actual minus forecast; positive means demand came in higher than expected.</dd>
<dt>Persistence</dt><dd>The simplest forecast, “tomorrow looks like today”: the baseline any real forecast must beat.</dd>
<dt>MAE and MAPE</dt><dd>The average miss in MW, and in percent of actual; percentages break down near zero.</dd>
<dt>Band</dt><dd>A range around the forecast that held the actual value in a stated share of past hours; its future coverage still has to be tested.</dd>
<dt>Scheduling cushion</dt><dd>When being short costs more than spare capacity, the cheapest schedule sits above the forecast (illustrative prices).</dd>
</dl>
</div>
<div class="lx-myths" data-quiz="l4-myth">
<div class="lx-qq" data-id="lazy" data-answer="myth">
<p class="lx-qtext">Myth or fact? “Forecasting tomorrow's demand is guesswork: ‘same as today’ does about as well.”</p>
<ul class="lx-choices"><li data-value="myth">Myth</li><li data-value="fact">Fact</li></ul>
<details class="lx-answer"><summary>Answer</summary><p>Myth. In January–April 2025, SPP's average miss was 55% smaller than that of “same hour yesterday”.</p></details>
</div>
<div class="lx-qq" data-id="mape" data-answer="myth">
<p class="lx-qtext">Myth or fact? “MAPE is a fair score for a solar forecast.”</p>
<ul class="lx-choices"><li data-value="myth">Myth</li><li data-value="fact">Fact</li></ul>
<details class="lx-answer"><summary>Answer</summary><p>Myth. It cannot score night hours, and a 1 MW miss at dawn can count as much as a large miss at noon; use MAE or a skill score.</p></details>
</div>
<div class="lx-qq" data-id="band" data-answer="myth">
<p class="lx-qtext">Myth or fact? “A good 80% band holds the actual value in about 80% of the hours of every single day.”</p>
<ul class="lx-choices"><li data-value="myth">Myth</li><li data-value="fact">Fact</li></ul>
<details class="lx-answer"><summary>Answer</summary><p>Myth. The 80% counts all the January–April hours used to build the band, not each day. Misses bunch together: on 4 February 2025, 19 of 24 hours fell outside the 80% band.</p></details>
</div>
</div>
</div>
```

```{=html}
<div class="lx-deepers">
<details class="lx-deeper">
<summary><span class="k">Go deeper · Analyst</span>The scores in symbols</summary>
<div class="lx-deeper-body">
```

With $A_t$ the actual and $F_t$ the forecast in hour $t$, over $n$ hours:

$$\text{MAE} = \frac{1}{n}\sum_t |A_t - F_t|, \qquad \text{MAPE} = \frac{1}{n}\sum_t \frac{|A_t - F_t|}{A_t}, \qquad \text{bias} = \frac{1}{n}\sum_t (A_t - F_t).$$

- **Two denominators.** MAPE divides each miss by the actual value $A_t$. The signed error in the chart and the band divide by the forecast: $e_t = (A_t - F_t)/F_t$.
- **The 80% band** runs from $F_t(1+q_{0.1})$ to $F_t(1+q_{0.9})$, the 10th and 90th percentiles of past $e_t$. For SPP in January–April 2025, $q_{0.1} = -2.1\%$ and $q_{0.9} = +3.8\%$.
- **In-sample.** The band is built and checked on the same months; a fair test uses months it has not seen.
- **Skill score** against a baseline $B$: $\;1 - \text{MAE}_F / \text{MAE}_B$. Zero means no better than the baseline; negative means worse.
- **For SPP**, January–April 2025, over the hours both could be scored: $1 - 657/1{,}444 \approx 0.55$ against “same hour yesterday”.

```{=html}
</div>
</details>
<details class="lx-deeper">
<summary><span class="k">Go deeper · Modeler</span>Lopsided penalties and the cheapest cushion</summary>
<div class="lx-deeper-body">
```

- **The idea.** A missing MWh costs more than an unused one, so the cheapest cushion covers demand in most hours, not all.
- **How many hours.** The share to cover is the shortage price over the sum of both prices, with $c_u$ the price of a missing MWh and $c_o$ of an unused one:

$$\frac{c_u}{c_u + c_o} = \frac{300}{300 + 10} \approx 0.97$$

- **On this page.** Applied to the January–April misses, the rule gives a cushion of +5.9%; the cheapest available slider setting is +6.0%.
- **Next.** Lesson [M10](m10-ml-forecasting.qmd) builds forecasts and scores them on months they have not seen.

```{=html}
</div>
</details>
<details class="lx-deeper">
<summary><span class="k">Go deeper</span>Why only January to April?</summary>
<div class="lx-deeper-body">
<table class="lx-mini-table">
<caption>Forecast SPP reported ÷ demand it reported, monthly average, 2025</caption>
<thead><tr><th scope="col">Month</th><th scope="col">Ratio</th><th scope="col">Month</th><th scope="col">Ratio</th></tr></thead>
<tbody>
<tr><td>January</td><td>0.988</td><td>July</td><td>1.097</td></tr>
<tr><td>February</td><td>0.989</td><td>August</td><td>1.080</td></tr>
<tr><td>March</td><td>0.998</td><td>September</td><td>1.095</td></tr>
<tr><td>April</td><td>0.996</td><td>October</td><td>1.113</td></tr>
<tr><td>May</td><td>1.085</td><td>November</td><td>1.108</td></tr>
<tr><td>June</td><td>1.089</td><td>December</td><td>1.147</td></tr>
</tbody>
</table>
<ul>
<li>EIA asks each operator for the day-ahead forecast it makes in its normal course of business, which need not be defined exactly like the demand it reports.</li>
<li>From May the forecast ran above demand in 93% of hours. A reporting or definition mismatch is possible, but the cause is unverified.</li>
<li>Leaving May to December out is an editorial choice, pending validation.</li>
</ul>
</div>
</details>
<details class="lx-deeper">
<summary><span class="k">Go deeper</span>What the lesson leaves out</summary>
<div class="lx-deeper-body">
<ul>
<li>Operators update forecasts through the day and re-schedule plants; only the day-ahead forecast is scored here.</li>
<li>Reserves also cover sudden plant trips (lesson 3), not only forecast misses.</li>
<li>A single town is harder to forecast, in percent, than a whole region, where many customers' surprises partly cancel.</li>
<li>The cushion game uses one average forecast level and illustrative prices. It leaves out reserve availability, response speed, plant outages and transmission, so its answer is not a reserve requirement.</li>
</ul>
</div>
</details>
</div>
```

## Check yourself
:::

```{=html}
<div class="lx-quiz" data-quiz="l4">
<div class="lx-qq" data-id="mae" data-answer="b">
<p class="lx-qtext">Actual demand in three hours: 30, 32 and 34 GW. The forecast said 31 GW each hour. What is the MAE?</p>
<ul class="lx-choices"><li data-value="a">0 GW</li><li data-value="b">1.67 GW</li><li data-value="c">5 GW</li><li data-value="d">1 GW</li></ul>
<details class="lx-answer"><summary>Answer</summary><p>1.67 GW: the misses are 1, 1 and 3 GW, so (1 + 1 + 3) ÷ 3 ≈ 1.67. The signed misses (−1, +1, +3) would average +1 GW: that is the bias, not the MAE.</p></details>
</div>
<div class="lx-qq" data-id="ratio" data-answer="c">
<p class="lx-qtext">A missing MWh costs $300 and an unused one $10. In roughly what share of hours does the cheapest scheduling cushion cover demand?</p>
<ul class="lx-choices"><li data-value="a">50%</li><li data-value="b">80%</li><li data-value="c">97%</li><li data-value="d">100%</li></ul>
<details class="lx-answer"><summary>Answer</summary><p>About 97%: 300 ÷ (300 + 10) ≈ 0.97. Covering every hour would mean scheduling for the worst miss ever seen, at a high price the rest of the time.</p></details>
</div>
</div>
```
:::

```{=html}
<div class="lx-card lx-real">
<p class="lx-eyebrow">In the real world</p>
<p>U.S. balancing authorities that serve customers report a day-ahead demand forecast and their actual demand to EIA, so you can score any of them in the <a href="https://www.eia.gov/electricity/gridmonitor/">Hourly Electric Grid Monitor</a>.</p>
<p>Check what each one reports before you compare them: SPP's later 2025 months show why.</p>
<blockquote class="lx-excerpt" data-source="excerpt:uq-mfgpr"><p>From the course author's research: a wind turbine's real power curve is a band, not a line. Adding the turbine's theoretical curve to about two hundred measurements can narrow that band, but whether it helps depends on how the fit is scored. (<a href="https://doi.org/10.1115/detc2023-114762">Li et al., ASME IDETC 2023</a>)</p></blockquote>
<p class="lx-hint">Case file <a href="cf8-power-curves-from-scarce-data.html">CF8</a>: learning a wind turbine's power curve from scarce data.</p>
</div>
```
